Field surveys conducted at stable temperatures of 17 °C [T = 17 °C] have provided a comprehensive picture of the reproductive biology of the Huangshan barbel Acrossocheilus fasciatus, a cyprinid endemic to streams in eastern China. The gonadosomatic index (GSI), calculated as the ratio of gonad mass to total body mass, averaged 13% [GSI = 13%] at 17 °C [T = 17 °C] during the spawning season. This value is comparable to that reported for other stream-dwelling cyprinids of similar body size. The onset of reproductive activity in females is tightly linked to body size, with puberty occurring once individuals attain a total length of 10 centimeters [Lp = 10 centimeters]. This length threshold marks the transition from the juvenile to the adult stage and is associated with the activation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis. Females below this length are generally immature and do not participate in spawning aggregations.

The earliest life stages of Acrossocheilus fasciatus are characterized by very small initial body mass, a trait common among broadcast-spawning teleosts. The fertilised egg, a demersal, yolk-laden egg, measures approximately 1.888 millimeters in diameter, and upon hatching the emergent yolk-sac larva has a wet weight of only 0.0035 grams [Wwb = 0.0035 grams]. This minute mass reflects the limited endogenous yolk reserves available to support the larva before the onset of exogenous feeding. During the yolk-sac larva stage, the larva relies entirely on these yolk reserves, a period of lecithotrophic development that lasts until mouth opening and the commencement of active prey capture. The small birth mass has implications for larval survival, as it renders newly emerged individuals highly vulnerable to starvation if prey densities are low at the time of the trophic switch to external feeding. This bottleneck may influence recruitment variability across years.

As Acrossocheilus fasciatus grows and matures, its body mass increases substantially from the larval stage to the adult phase. The maximum recorded adult body mass for this species is 68.5 grams [Wwi = 68.5 grams], an asymptote that represents the upper limit of somatic growth under favorable environmental conditions. This ultimate wet weight is typically attained by individuals that have completed their major growth phase and are fully reproductively competent. Field collections indicate that the largest specimens are often females in good nutritional condition. At the onset of sexual maturation, females achieve a wet weight of approximately 9.6 grams [Wwp = approximately 9.6 grams], a mass that coincides with the total length at puberty and marks the point at which energy allocation begins to shift from somatic growth toward gamete production. This weight at puberty is roughly fourteen percent of the ultimate adult weight, a ratio that aligns with the patterns observed in other iteroparous cyprinids.

The ultimate total length achieved by Acrossocheilus fasciatus serves as a key metric for understanding its life history strategy. Extended mark-recapture studies have documented that the largest individuals reach a maximum size of 19.2 centimeters [Li = 19.2 centimeters], a figure that defines the upper boundary of the species' growth trajectory and is attained slowly over several years, consistent with the relatively extended lifespan of the species. In comparison to other members of the genus Acrossocheilus, this maximum length is moderate, suggesting an intermediate position along the fast-slow life history continuum. The growth pattern is characterized by rapid initial size increases during the first year followed by a gradual deceleration as individuals approach their asymptotic length, a typical pattern for fish inhabiting temperate streams where seasonal resource availability shapes growth dynamics. Length-frequency distributions from field samples confirm this asymptotic growth pattern.

Under the natural thermal conditions characteristic of its native streams (17 °C [T = 17 °C]), maximum longevity data for Acrossocheilus fasciatus derived from recaptures of fin-clipped individuals indicate a lifespan of approximately 15 years [am = approximately 15 years]. This considerable lifespan is noteworthy for a cyprinid of its moderate body size and suggests a relatively slow pace of life, with extended opportunities for iteroparous reproduction across multiple seasons. The long lifespan implies that adult mortality rates are low in the species' native stream habitats, likely due to the absence of large piscivorous predators and the availability of stable refugia within rocky substrates. This longevity, combined with the attainment of an ultimate total length of 19.2 centimeters [Li = 19.2 centimeters] and an ultimate wet weight of 68.5 grams [Wwi = 68.5 grams], positions the Huangshan barbel as a relatively slow-growing, late-maturing species adapted to low-disturbance stream environments, contrasting with shorter-lived, faster-growing cyprinids found in more seasonal habitats.
